title: AI agents are great at building game engines and terrible at humour. Devlog 1 of my rage platformer.
author: platoevolved
selftext:
For the last 6 months my main build tools have been Claude Code and OpenCode. Current project: IMP: Not a Troll, a rage platformer inspired by Level Devil, the Poki game with millions of plays. Original art, original levels, same core idea. Two inputs, move and jump, and a dungeon that hates you.

First, credit where it's due. The agents built essentially everything systematic: the engine, physics and collision, 14 trap types (vanishing floors, control reversal, gravity shifts, fake exits), coyote time, jump buffering. The whole game core is a pure function with Vitest tests, so the agents verify their own changes before showing me. There's a validator that fails the build if a level can't be finished.

Then the wall: the levels themselves. I tried, repeatedly, to get the agents to design fun troll levels. They never really got it. Every set they generated came out technically valid and completely flat. Traps placed where traps go, no sense of theatre. A good troll moment is misdirection with a fair tell. The fun is the second you realise you were played, and getting that timing right is taste, not rules.

Everything codable, the agents did. Fun, they couldn't.

Strange that Star Trek got it right with Data having real trouble understanding humour 🤣.

So I flipped the workflow. Asked the agents to build a level editor instead, which they did, a dev-gated builder with export and tests. Every level in the game is now designed by hand, by me, inside the tools the agents built.

The takeaway so far: agents are best at the systems layer and the tools layer, and the fun-design layer stayed stubbornly human. I stopped trying to prompt taste into a generator, and the game got good the week I started drawing levels myself.

Clip is 30 seconds of the game being horrible to me. Happy to go deeper on any part of the setup.
